passages.t: ‘Restore us, O God’: the vine God planted
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. To the tune of ‘The Lilies of the Covenant.’ A Psalm of Asaph” (verse 1). The prayer opens, “Hear us, O Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock” (verse 1). It asks God to come and save (verse 2).

Three times a chorus returns, each time a little fuller. “Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved” (verse 3). Then ‘O God of Hosts’ (verse 7). Then ‘O LORD God of Hosts’ (verse 19).

In between, the people complain. God has fed them “with the bread of tears” (verse 5). Their enemies mock them (verse 6).

Then comes a picture. “You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it” (verse 8). The vine filled the land and spread from the sea to the river (verses 9 to 11). Now its walls are broken down. Passers-by strip it, and wild boars tear it up (verses 12 to 13). “Your vine has been cut down and burned” (verse 16). The people ask God to set his hand on “the son of man You have raised up for Yourself” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
‘Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh’ (verse 2) were tribes of the north. Ephraim and Manasseh were the sons of Joseph. So many scholars connect this psalm with the days when Assyria crushed the northern kingdom of Israel. Some think it was prayed in Judah for the northern tribes. The psalm itself names no year.

The chorus would sound familiar. It echoes the priests' blessing: “may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25). The people ask God to give them that blessing again.

Everyone in Israel knew vineyards. A vineyard had a stone wall around it. Break the wall, and anyone walking by could pick the grapes, and animals could trample the vines. The vine was a familiar picture of Israel. God brought it out of Egypt, planted it in the land and cared for it. So the question is sharp: why would the gardener let his own vine be torn up?

‘The man at Your right hand’ (verse 17) may be the king, or Israel itself, called God's ‘son’ in Exodus 4:22.
passages.later:
Isaiah sang a song of God's vineyard, which gave sour grapes (Isaiah 5:1-2). Jesus told a story of a vineyard and its tenants (Mark 12:1).

On the night before he died, Jesus took up the picture for himself. “I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard” (John 15:1). “I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit” (John 15:5). Christians read Psalm 80's plea for the vine, and for the ‘son of man’ at God's right hand, in the light of Jesus, who called himself the Son of Man.
passages.asks:
Have you watched something God planted get broken down: a family, a church, a friendship? Psalm 80 lets you ask God why, and ask him to come back to what is his.

The chorus is a prayer you can learn by heart: ‘Restore us, O God; make Your face shine on us, that we may be saved.’ Notice that it asks for God's face before it asks for anything else.
